title: The most wonderful thing
hookLine: the year's summit sit: Yudhishthira at the lake, and the wonder of how the living forget death

cards: Day six hundred ninety-seven: a king's snake sacrifice, and a storyteller who begins the story of the Bharatas. That's where this year started. Since then: a war, a song, a child in Vraja, the saints.
Today, the summit sit, and one scene. Five brothers in the forest, desperately thirsty. One finds a lake.
A voice from the water says: answer my questions first, then drink. He drinks anyway, and falls. So does the next brother, and the next, and the next.

teach.b: Then the eldest, Yudhishthira, reaches the shore and finds his four brothers lying still. He doesn't drink. He says: ask.
The voice, a yaksha, a spirit of the lake, asks question after question.

teach.h: WHAT IS THE MOST WONDERFUL THING?
teach.b: One of them: what is the most wonderful thing? His answer, in paraphrase: every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and the ones who remain want to stay forever. What could be more wonderful than that?
His wonder isn't at death. It's at forgetting: we see it every day and live as if it isn't coming. Then the yaksha offers him one brother back, his choice.
He picks Nakula, a son of his father's other wife, not mighty Bhima or Arjuna, so that Madri, too, will have a living son, as his own mother Kunti does.
And the yaksha shows who he is: Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's own father, testing him. He gives all four brothers back. Here's the teaching.

In Hindu thought the body is passing, and dharma, right living, is what you do with the time; remembering death isn't gloom, it's what makes the right choice clear. Hindu families build that remembering into the year.
Just before Navaratri comes Pitru Paksha, a fortnight for the ancestors, when many families offer water, sesame and food in memory of those who have gone, often with a share set out for the crows.
The living forget, Yudhishthira said; these days are for not forgetting.

how: Yudhishthira's answers to the yaksha in the Mahabharata's Vana Parva are retold in Hindu homes and talks, and in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight before Navaratri, many families offer water, sesame and food in memory of their ancestors.

o: the year of Rama's exile and the road to Lanka
the year of the great story, the saints and the teachers
the year spent only on the Vedas and Upanishads

p: chosen, so Madri would have a living son
the god behind the voice, testing his son
a fortnight to remember the ancestors

s: Yudhishthira's wonder was simply that people die
his wonder was that the living see death every day and still act as if they'll stay forever.
Yudhishthira chose to bring back Nakula, Madri's son
so Madri, too, would have a living son. the voice was Dharma, testing him, and gave all four back.
Pitru Paksha comes just before Navaratri
a fortnight when many families remember their ancestors with water, sesame and food.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the voice offers one of your four brothers back to life, your choice. who?
o: Bhima, the strongest, to win the war ahead.
Nakula, so your father's other wife also has a living son.
Arjuna, the archer everyone loves most.
games.why: he chose dharma over advantage. the voice was Dharma himself, his father, and he gave all four brothers back.

practice: Hold a glass of water. Families who keep Pitru Paksha may know tarpan, water offered in memory of those who have gone; this is a small way in its spirit.
Bring one person to mind, from your family or your life, say their name, and pour a little of the water into a plant or onto the earth. Notice the breath still coming: you remain, for now.

If you pray, give thanks for them in words you already use; if you don't, let the water be the thanks. If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Year three. The great story, the child in Vraja, the saints and the teachers, held together by the ones who remain.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ashcharya, a wonder. The word in the Yaksha's question: what is the most wonderful thing?

carryVoice: Your line: we remain only for now. Yudhishthira's wonder was how easily we forget it. Go gently.
